title: Stage 1 on the GPU, bulk first: the device tests the whole matrix, the host applies the findings in today's order
summary:
Design from the angle "bulk on the device, tail on the host", with today's sequential cascade kept as host engine and reference. Nothing was implemented and nothing in the project tree was changed.

What I read: state.hpp and numerics.hpp in full; presolve.cpp 60-515; rules.hpp 1-160; rules_propagation.cpp, rules_bounds.cpp, implied.hpp; state_ops.cpp 14-323; rules_rows.cpp 40-279; rules_tightening.cpp 52-353; rules_singleton_cols.cpp 398-592; three parts of rules_parallel_rows.cpp; hash.cpp 20-139; DESIGN.md amendment A11 and sections 2 to 4; the data layout, kernel and round sections of stage1b_design/final_design.txt; STAGE0_REPORT.md section 6; ASSUMPTIONS AS-302 to AS-310; HISTORY entries 32 and 51. What I ran: three scripts over the measurement agent's CSV files and the stored node summary, and one probe build of my own (a scratch copy of commit 04692babd with counters in the row rules and in bound propagation, run on the 240 benchmark dumps; its hash equals the stored node run on 240 of 240).

The main result of the probe (240 benchmark instances): a visit whose row was not listed again since the family took its list sees exactly the state at the start of the list. Such visits without any effect are 87.2% of the row-rule visits (68.6% of that family's work) and 77.7% of the propagation visits (78.6% of its work); another 16.5% of the propagation work is visits that only write an implied-bound record. Visits of rows that were listed again are 2.3% and 1.4% of the visits (3.8% and 2.7% of the work).

The design built on it: the device computes everything that is a function of the state at the start of a step (the state build, a "no effect" certificate with its work count for every listed row or column, parallel-row keys and their sort, collection lists, implied-bound records, the reduced model, the hash). The host keeps today's loops and skips certified rows that were not listed again; every finding is applied by today's code in today's order. Consequences: a run with and without a GPU, on any GPU type, gives the same bits, and no threshold can change a result. Against today's engine only two things change, both with a switch and both measurable on the host alone: the hash function (a chain cannot be computed in parallel) and, recommended, the rule for implied-bound records (best candidate instead of first-come with a step), which can only tighten.

Where the angle breaks: (1) on x86 the host needs a full copy of the state for its tail, so the state build stays limited by host memory (2.0 to 2.1 times measured, about 3.3 with huge pages); (2) the application of findings stays sequential on the host, which is 9% of today's seconds on the 240 by my arithmetic and more on the nine large instances, so a second step (device application of whole scripts) is needed there; (3) the screen saves little where a host visit already costs O(1) (row rules, dual fixing); (4) below about 2e5 nonzeros the device is not used. My projection, by arithmetic on measured shares and not by a run: about 2.5 times on the 240 and 2.0 to 2.4 times on the nine instances above 1e7 nonzeros on x86, more with huge pages and with device application.
design:
0. TERMS
Bulk step: the part of one family call (or of one take of its list) that the device computes on the state as the step found it (S0). Certificate: one byte per listed row or column saying "today's visit of this item on S0 changes nothing", with the work units w0 that visit would have spent. Clean: the item was not put on the family's list again between the take and its turn. Ordered walk: today's loop over the list, in today's order, which skips certified clean items and runs today's visit code on all others. Mirror: the device copy of the state on x86. Journal: marks of what the host changed since the last sync. Reference backend: the plain C++ form of every device function, used for tests and for builds without CUDA.

1. PRINCIPLE
The device never decides the order of anything. It computes pure functions of S0; the host applies. For a clean item, S0 is the state today's visit would have seen, so a certified clean item can be skipped with its work charged, and the result is the one of today's engine, bit for bit. A row that an earlier finding touched is listed again by the state's own events; the host visits it with today's code at its turn, as today. So today's Gauss-Seidel order, the list orders, the incremental activities, the budgets, the record stack and all 22 order dependences of the inventory stay where they are: on the host.
Sketch of the walk (it is today's loop with one test added):
  for k in list order:
    if budget.stop(): push the rest back; return stopped
    r = rows[k]; if not alive[r]: continue
    if cert[k] == NO_EFFECT and not (pending[r] & own_list): budget.spend(w0[k]); continue
    visit(r)   // today's code, unchanged
A certificate may be conservative (say "host" when unsure); it must never be wrong. The rule for implied-bound records is the one exception, see 4.

2. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT SAYS ABOUT THIS SPLIT
- My probe, 240 benchmark instances, counts from one deterministic run: row rules 19,343,168 visits: clean without effect 87.2% of visits and 68.6% of work, clean with an effect 10.5% and 27.7%, listed again 2.3% and 3.8%; 85.9% of the findings come from clean visits. Bound propagation 15,616,135 visits: clean without effect 77.7% and 78.6%, clean record only 19.4% and 16.5%, clean with a bound change 1.5% and 2.1%, listed again 1.4% and 2.7%. Visits that only refresh an activity or only set a mark: none in the row rules, below 0.05% in propagation. Per instance the listed-again share of the work has median 0.0%, 90th percentile 10.2% (row rules) and 9.7% (propagation), largest 65.6% (supportcase7) and 58.1% (ns1952667).
- From the measurement agent (240): 91.8% of the work units of the six families other than the doubleton rule lie outside the visits that make a finding; tightening has chain length at most 2 (the same row again), dual fixing, parallel rows and the doubleton rule 1.
- Lists and calls by size, my script over the agent's CSV (240, Mac seconds): with a threshold of 100,000 work units, 1,499 of 8,257 lists and calls (18%) hold 93.2% of the rule seconds; median 6 and at most 40 such steps per instance. At 200,000: 1,121 steps with 89.3%. At 20,000: 2,616 steps with 98.0%, of which 834 take the host less than 100 microseconds.

3. STATE AND MEMORY
- Host: state_t as it is. Two changes of form, none of content: the large arrays come from a presolve-owned memory resource (so that arrays built on the device are moved in without a zero fill, huge pages can be asked for, and Grace Hopper can use managed memory), and every mutating operation sets a journal mark when a device is attached.
- Device image on x86: the same arrays with the same slots (both stores with start, used, capacity, size, index, value, twin; row and column scalars; both activities). Slot identity makes inf_slot, twins and tombstones the host's, so a hand-over is a copy and every array can be compared in tests. Load balancing is an index, not a storage order: row ids and column ids sorted by length class (stable device sort), with the class boundaries of cuOpt's load-balanced code (sub-warp groups up to 64 entries, one block above, split of very long lines). Whether storage in class order would be faster is a kernel benchmark, not a result question.
- Device-only arrays: infinite-term counts as two uint16_t arrays derived from the host's int32 counts, saturating; a row with a saturated count is never certified (review rule of cuOpt PR 2372, without changing the host). Listed and stale flags, certificate and w0 per item, sort and candidate scratch.
- Bytes: 40 per nonzero for the image, about 135 per row and 95 per column; during the build 28 more per nonzero (uploaded CSR 12, sort keys and positions 16). For 2.57e8 nonzeros about 10.3 GB plus 7.2 GB at the peak. A byte budget is an option; when the plan does not fit, or an allocation fails, the call runs on the host with the same result.
- Sync on x86, host to device: the journal marks rows and columns whose scalars changed, lines whose entries changed and columns whose layout changed (move_entry). Before a bulk step the marked data is copied through pinned staging and scattered; integer arrays that are functions of the rest (sizes, locks, row_free_size, row_singletons, counts) are derived on the device and compared in assertion builds. Three ways, all with the same result: no sync and the marked items go to the host (they are on its lists anyway), marked data only, or the whole image. After a host rebuild the device repeats the rebuild on its image and receives the scalars of marked rows, or receives the image whole.
- Sync on x86, device to host: in the base plan only the state build (whole arrays) and small results (flags, keys, orders, records). 
- Grace Hopper: one managed slab, preferred location device, accessed-by host, the host_access and release pair of the Stage 1b design; no mirror and no sync. Functional only until a node is measured.
- Work lists and the record stack exist on the host only. The device gets a taken list as an int32 array.

4. THE TWO CHANGES AGAINST TODAY'S ENGINE (each a switch, each measured on the host alone first)
- Hash: model_hash is a chain and cannot be parallel. New form: per array the sum modulo 2^64 of mix(word xor mix(index + array seed)), the per-array sums chained as today. A sum of integers has no order. The stored hashes are replaced once; the old chain stays available for the transition.
- Implied-bound records of continuous columns: today a record is replaced when a candidate beats it by a step, in visit order, so the result depends on the order and a certificate cannot cover a row that would write one (16.5% of the propagation work on the 240; more than half of the propagation work on 46 of the 240 instances, more than 90% on 19). New rule, in every mode: each propagation list is served in two phases. Phase 1, pure: for every listed row the candidates on S0; per column and side the best one, equal values to the smaller row index, replaces the valid record when it is better; marks are a union. Phase 2: the ordered walk; rows it visits apply the same best-candidate rule. A record is then at least as tight as today's (it is at least every candidate today's rule saw). budget.found() is called for a certified row when it is the source of a record changed in phase 1. Without this change the device still certifies the rows that write nothing; the host then keeps the record-writing visits.

5. PARTS (short; the table per part is in per_part)
- State build: device from the size threshold: upload, column histogram and prefix sum, stable radix sort of entry positions by column (the code that exists, bit-equal in 3,734 builds), locks, row_singletons, both activities by fold kernels in the host's lane order (fold_light and fold_block of the Stage 1b design, to be built), then one download into moved-in host arrays. The start step runs on the host afterwards (0.2% of the seconds).
- Tightening, dual fixing, the singleton-column rules, the row rules: certificate by a dry run of the visit (arithmetic from shared headers, one thread per line up to 64 entries, one block above with the map parts as integer, any, min and max reductions and the sequential parts on one thread); ordered walk on the host.
- Bound propagation: a row kernel for "an integer column would be tightened" and "the guard asks for a fresh sum", a column kernel for the records (reduction of value and row pairs under a total order), from the structure of cuOpt's load-balanced kernels; activities are the host's, read from the mirror, so no fold is needed per step.
- Parallel rows: keys of all listed rows (an integer sum per row and a minimum for the reference column), stable radix sort of (hash, core length, row), bucket links; the pair scan in the buckets stays on the host.
- Doubleton rule and simple probing: collection on the device (order-preserving selection), forest, composition and substitution on the host in the base plan.
- Output: reduced model and hash on the device from the mirror; inside cuOpt the result can stay on the device.
- Driver, lists, record stack, postsolve: host.

6. SECOND STEP: DEVICE APPLICATION OF WHOLE SCRIPTS
A script is the list of state operations of a step in the order the host would apply them. For families whose findings do not depend on each other inside a call (dual fixing, make_explicit, tightening edits, parallel-row merges, the substitution of an alias batch, zero-cost singleton columns) the script is known before anything is applied. The device can replay it with the host's bits because every order-dependent value belongs to one line: the activity and the sides of a row are replayed by that row in script order, the cost and the appended entries of a column by that column, lists by a first-touch key (integer minimum, then a sort), record offsets by a prefix sum; the objective offset is a chain of k terms and stays on the host. This is built only where the host application is measured above 2% of the hybrid time of a size class, and on x86 it pays only for dense scripts, because the host copy must follow (whole scalar arrays are copied at 18 GB/s; single entries cost the host as much as applying them).

7. WHERE THIS ANGLE BREAKS
- x86 host memory: the tail runs today's code on state_t, so the host must hold the whole state from the first row-rule call on. The state build is then limited by the host creating its arrays (measured: 2.0 to 2.1 times end to end on 15 instances, 3.3 with huge pages), not by the device (40 to 48 ms for 2.57e8 nonzeros).
- Application in host order cannot be given to the device for the cascades (row rules, propagation, singleton-column cascade) without giving up today's order: an exact parallel form would have to commit prefixes of the list, one prefix per row that reads what an earlier row wrote.
- The certificate saves little where today's visit is O(1): row rules (40 ns per visit) and dual fixing (9 ns per column).
- Two copies on x86 need the journal and the sync; Grace Hopper does not.
- If the owner wants the applications of the cascades on the device as well, the order has to become a snapshot order (rounds from one state). That is another design: it loses equality with today's engine, needs more rounds (1.4 times on average and up to 22 times for propagation in Sofranac, Gleixner and Pokutta 2022, section 2.2, quoted from this round's research report, not read by me), and its reference would be a new host engine.

8. FILES OF THIS WORK
/private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-acoerduek--claude-spares-spare-bsnTJo/c660eb6b-7edc-4afc-bf62-0442cb32d870/scratchpad/gpu_s1_design/design_bulk-first/thresholds.py, nmin.py, probe_agg.py, probe_agg2.py, and the directory probe (scratch copy with counters, build, one output pair per instance).

per_part.runs_on: Device from the model threshold (provisional 2e5 nonzeros), host below it.
per_part.device_algorithm: Upload of the CSR and the row and column arrays; column histogram and prefix sum; stable radix sort (CUB) of the entry positions by column for csc.index, csc.value and both twins; locks by integer sums; row_singletons by a map over columns; both activities of every row by fold kernels in the host's lane order (lane groups up to 64 entries, one block with 256 lanes above, tree fixed by entry position, infinite terms counted in the scan with one integer atomic only when nonzero); lists are an iota and are not built on the device. One download into host arrays that are moved into state_t. About 12 to 15 launches, one upload (12 bytes per nonzero), one download (40 bytes per nonzero plus scalars).
per_part.why_host: Below the threshold: the host builds 1e5 nonzeros in about 4 ms (40.4 ns per nonzero, 240 benchmark instances, node); the measured device path lost below 8.5e5 nonzeros as a first call in a fresh process. The crossover with a warm context and pooled memory is not measured.
per_part.same_result_as_today: Yes, every array bit-equal. Shown for the transpose, twins and locks (3,734 builds); the fold kernels are designed and not built.
per_part.conflict_rule: None: no two rows or columns interact.
per_part.expected_gain: State build is 31.4% of the seconds on the 240 and 34.2% on the 9 instances above 1e7 nonzeros (node). Measured end to end 2.0 to 2.1 times (15 instances), about 3.3 times with huge pages; the limit is the host creating its arrays.

per_part.device_algorithm: None in the base plan. With script application (second step) the decisions are a map over rows and columns and the activity updates a replay per row in storage order.
per_part.why_host: 0.048 s of 19.467 s, 0.2% (240, node); 0.191 s on the 9 large instances. Its changes reach activities through two-term updates in column order.

per_part.part: Row rules: empty row, infeasible row, redundant row, singleton row, forcing row
per_part.runs_on: Both. Device certificate for a list above the step threshold; ordered walk on the host; lists below the threshold are today's loop.
per_part.device_algorithm: One map over the listed rows on row scalars only (free size, sides, both activities with counts, update counts and largest term): NO_EFFECT when the row is not empty, not stale, not infeasible, not redundant, has more than one free entry and fails the O(1) part of the forcing test on both sides; everything else is left to the host. w0 is 8 for a certified row. One launch, one compaction or a flag download of one byte per row.
per_part.why_host: The application: a tightened or fixed column changes what later rows read, so the order is part of today's result. Rows with an effect or listed again hold 31.5% of the family's work (240, my probe), at most 0.31 s or 1.6% of today's seconds if time follows work.
per_part.same_result_as_today: Yes, bit for bit: certified clean rows are visits without effect, all others run today's code in today's order.
per_part.conflict_rule: None on the device. On the host today's rule: the first row in list order wins, the next one sees its result.
per_part.expected_gain: Small: a visit without effect costs the host about 40 ns. At most 68.6% of 5.1% of the seconds (240).

per_part.part: Bound propagation and the switch to explicit bounds
per_part.runs_on: Both. Device for phase 1 of a list above the step threshold; ordered walk on the host; short lists on the host. make_explicit on the host in the base plan.
per_part.device_algorithm: Row kernel over the listed rows: per side the host's tests (side readable, 0 or 1 infinite term, the candidate of each entry from the stored activity with the residual first, the error guard), flag CHANGE when an integer column would be tightened after rounding or, after the switch, a continuous one would take a step, flag REFRESH when the guard drops a candidate and the activity is not fresh, w0 from the row scalars. Column kernel: per column and side the best candidate with its row (reduction of pairs under a total order, any tree), compared with the valid record; marks as a union; a flag for the rows that hold a new record. Scheduling from cuOpt's load-balanced kernels; arithmetic from implied.hpp and numerics.hpp. Two to four launches, one read-back, flags and changed records down.
per_part.why_host: Bound changes are applied before the next row is tested and the 16 steps per bound are counted in visit order. Rows with a bound change or listed again hold 4.8% of the family's work (240, my probe), about 0.15 s or 0.8% of the seconds. Chains: the longest is 834 levels (neos-1122047) in lists of a few thousand rows, which stay below the step threshold.
per_part.same_result_as_today: Bound changes, order and budgets: yes. Records: only with the record rule left as today, and then the device share falls from 95.1% to 78.6% of the family's work. With the recommended best-candidate rule a record is at least as tight as today's and the explicit bounds made from it can differ by up to one step.
per_part.conflict_rule: Records: larger lower and smaller upper candidate win, equal values go to the smaller row index. Bounds: host order.
per_part.expected_gain: 16.4% of the seconds on the 240, 10.1% on the 9 large instances; up to 95% of it leaves the host.

per_part.part: Row tightening: integral scaling with gcd, side rounding, coefficient strengthening
per_part.runs_on: Both: device certificate, host walk that runs today's visit on flagged rows.
per_part.device_algorithm: Dry run of the visit per listed row: scan (counts, all-integer test, the compensated sum of fixed terms in storage order), the scale search as the host's sequential walk with its early exits, the rounded sides, the strengthening test as an any-reduction over the entries. NO_EFFECT with w0 (8 plus one to four times the used slots, by the path taken). One thread per row up to 64 entries, one block above; a sequential part longer than a set length without an exit hands the row to the host.
per_part.why_host: The edits themselves: 8.6% of the family's work is in visits with an edit (240), about 0.25 s or 1.3% of the seconds. Candidate for script application, since no edit reads another row.
per_part.conflict_rule: None: a row reads and writes itself; column bounds are not written by this family.
per_part.expected_gain: 15.1% of the seconds on the 240, 10.0% on the 9 large; about 91% of it leaves the host.

per_part.runs_on: Both: device flags, host fixes the flagged columns in list order.
per_part.device_algorithm: A map over the listed columns on cost, lock counts and bounds. One launch.
per_part.why_host: The fixings write activities and the objective offset in list order. The whole family is 0.6% of the seconds on the 240 and 2.7% on the 9 large (39,899,589 fixings), where script application is the remedy.
per_part.conflict_rule: None: a fixing changes no lock and no cost.
per_part.expected_gain: Below 0.5% on the 240; on the 9 large only with script application.

per_part.runs_on: Both: keys, sort and bucket links on the device; pair scan, merges and subtractions on the host.
per_part.device_algorithm: Per listed row with at least two free entries: number of core entries, the core entry in the smallest column (minimum reduction), the sum of entry_hash(column, a divided by that coefficient) as an integer sum; then a stable radix sort of (hash, core length, row) and the neighbour links. Keys and the order are downloaded (16 bytes per row). The walk charges the keys per row and stops where today's loop stops.
per_part.why_host: The scan inside a bucket is a chain (a merge changes what the next comparison reads, the limit of 4 unlike neighbours is counted while rows are deleted). Comparisons and reductions are 0.148 of 0.921 s of the family (240, Mac), about 1.6% of the seconds.
per_part.same_result_as_today: Yes: the key is an integer sum, the sort has the row as last key, so there is one order.
per_part.conflict_rule: None on the device. Host: the smaller index is kept, rows above first.
per_part.expected_gain: 10.2% of the seconds on the 240, 13.9% on the 9 large; about 80% of it (keys 62.5%, sort and links 17.5%, Mac split) leaves the host.

per_part.part: Doubleton rule with the alias forest
per_part.runs_on: Host in the base plan, except the collection. Substitution on the device in the second step.
per_part.device_algorithm: Collection: order-preserving selection of the listed equations with two free entries, their two entries and the right-hand side less the fixed terms. Second step: forest edges are the minimum spanning forest under list position, maps composed level by level from the root (one launch per level, the host's association order; pointer jumping would change the bits), substitution replayed per row in map order.
per_part.why_host: Collection is 11% of the family, the tree walk 6%, row deletion and substitution 79% (0.250 of 0.317 s; 240, Mac). The substitution sums coefficients, costs and side shifts in map order and decides slots and column layout. Whole family: 4.0% of the seconds on the 240, 5.9% on the 9 large.
per_part.same_result_as_today: Yes in the base plan. In the second step only with the column layout of move_entry reproduced, which is the hardest piece of this design.
per_part.conflict_rule: Host order. Second step: each row replays its own substituted entries in map order, so rows do not conflict.
per_part.expected_gain: None in the base plan (0.4% from the collection).

per_part.part: Singleton-column family: free singleton column on an equation and on an inequality, zero-cost singleton columns, forcing column
per_part.runs_on: Both: device certificate, host walk with today's code for the rest.
per_part.device_algorithm: Per listed column the O(1) forcing-column test; per listed row with a singleton column a dry run of the visit that certifies only outcomes without a history term (growth factors, the saved-entry limit and unreadable marks send the row to the host). The walk still writes the row's stamp for a certified row.
per_part.why_host: The cascade inside a call (a deleted row makes new singleton columns; one call finishes a chain of thirty equations) and the history of the call. The family is 1.3% of the seconds on the 240 and 6.0% on the 9 large (dlr2 4.2 s).
per_part.conflict_rule: Host order: the singleton column with the smallest index that passes.
per_part.expected_gain: At most 97.9% of the family's work lies outside finding visits (240); the certifiable share is smaller and not measured.

per_part.part: Simple probing on equations (built at edd147a7e, in review)
per_part.runs_on: Both: row tests on the device, batch building and substitution on the host.
per_part.device_algorithm: Per listed equation the tests that read the state as the call found it (at least three free entries, readable side, no infinite term, the balance test, the scan for binaries and the first binary that passes): a candidate list in list order.
per_part.why_host: A row is refused when the batch already connects two of its columns, which is greedy in list order; the application is that of the doubleton rule. 1.8% of the seconds in the one stored Mac run (240).

per_part.part: Parallel columns: fixing by dominance (R6) and merge (R9), designed and not built
per_part.runs_on: Both: keys and sort on the device, pair scan on the host as designed.
per_part.device_algorithm: The parallel-row key kernel on the other orientation (number of live entries, hash over row and coefficient divided by the coefficient in the smallest row), stable sort, bucket links; the group of singleton columns of a row sorted by cost over coefficient.
per_part.why_host: The designs apply one pair at a time with every premise computed at application; a merge changes the bounds of the kept column that later tests read. No measurement exists.
per_part.same_result_as_today: There is no built rule; the host rule as designed is the reference.
per_part.conflict_rule: As designed: ties to the smaller index.
per_part.expected_gain: Not measurable before the rule exists; by shape as the parallel rows.

per_part.part: Dual bound strengthening (R7) and the alias of single-lock columns (R8), designed and not built
per_part.runs_on: Both: certificate on the device, application on the host in index order.
per_part.device_algorithm: R7: column kernel with a maximum over the rows that lock the column against its cost, O(1) per row from the stored activities (the record kernel of propagation with another row filter). R8: map over rows for candidates.
per_part.why_host: R7: a new bound changes the activities later columns read. R8: one transaction per binary, then a substitution. No measurement exists.
per_part.same_result_as_today: The host rule as designed is the reference.

per_part.part: The five further rules: implied equation, implied integer with scaling, column stuffing, single equation, dominated column; designed and not built
per_part.runs_on: Both: certificate on the device, application on the host in index order.
per_part.device_algorithm: Implied equation: map over columns. Implied integer: count of live continuous columns per row (integer reduction), candidates, one walk per candidate. Stuffing: per row a small sort and a prefix test inside one thread. Single equation: two compensated sums per marked row in storage order. Dominated column: per row the two cheapest compensators per direction (minimum reductions of pairs), then per column a compensated sum in the column's storage order.
per_part.why_host: Each is designed with index order and first-wins rules (two columns pointing at one row; a conversion that leaves other rows with one continuous column; a fixing that changes prices). No measurement exists.
per_part.same_result_as_today: The host rule as designed is the reference.

per_part.device_algorithm: None. It chooses bulk step or host loop per call and per list.
per_part.why_host: Control flow without work of its own; the stall rule and the stop between two lines are kept exactly by the walk, which charges w0 for skipped items.
per_part.same_result_as_today: Yes, including work, first_work, stopped and limited.

per_part.part: Storage between phases: compaction of sparse lines, rebuild, absorbing fixed terms
per_part.runs_on: Host for its copy; the device keeps its image by the same operations. On Grace Hopper the device does it for both.
per_part.device_algorithm: Per listed line an order-preserving compaction with twin updates; rebuild as stable compaction of both stores; activities of compacted rows by the fold kernel, which has the host's bits.
per_part.why_host: On x86 the host copy has to be compacted at host memory speed whoever computes it; a download of the rebuilt image costs about what the host rebuild costs. 5.1% of the seconds on the 240, 4.2% on the 9 large.
per_part.same_result_as_today: Yes; the rebuild decision reads the host layout.
per_part.expected_gain: None on x86; the share on Grace Hopper is not measured.

per_part.device_algorithm: None in the base plan. In the second step a script is the record list of its step; saved rows are gathered on the device in script order with offsets by a prefix sum and appended on the host.
per_part.why_host: Appends in application order, timed inside the families. The undo is a chain by definition and runs outside the presolve call.

per_part.runs_on: Both: device above the model threshold when the mirror is current, host otherwise.
per_part.device_algorithm: New indices by two prefix sums, gather of the live entries, fixed terms per row as one compensated sum in storage order by one thread per row, sides by dd_residual, a segmented sort of the rows that are not in increasing column order, download of 12 bytes per reduced nonzero. Inside cuOpt the arrays can stay on the device.
per_part.why_host: When the last phase ran on the host and the mirror would need a full sync first.
per_part.expected_gain: 4.6% of the seconds on the 240, 4.0% on the 9 large; on x86 the download into new host memory limits it unless the model is much smaller or stays on the device.

per_part.runs_on: Device with the output, host otherwise; the same function on both.
per_part.device_algorithm: Per array an integer sum of mixed words keyed by position; about 12 reductions, or one kernel with the output.
per_part.why_host: Only when the output was written on the host; the sum form has no dependency chain and is also faster there.
per_part.same_result_as_today: No: another function, every stored hash is replaced once. No reduction changes. The old chain can be kept behind a switch at 5.5% of the seconds.
per_part.expected_gain: 5.5% of the seconds on the 240, 5.0% on the 9 large.

hybrid_rule:
No part of the rule can change a result, because the device only certifies visits without effect and computes values that have one definition. The numbers are still fixed constants in the options, the same on every machine, so that timings are repeatable.

1. Model: the device is used when CUDA is built in, the memory plan (a function of rows, columns and nonzeros) fits the byte budget option, and the model has at least N_min nonzeros. Provisional N_min = 200,000. Below it the call is today's engine untouched. On the 240 (node run) 143 instances lie below 2e5 with 6.7% of the summed seconds; the 50 between 5e4 and 2e5 take 15.3 ms in the median and 1.0 s together. N_min is fixed in milestone 4 as the smallest size from which no instance is slower.
2. Step: a call, or a take of a list inside a call, is a bulk step when its estimate (live entries of the listed rows plus 8 per row, from the list length and the average row length) times the family's cost per unit exceeds four times the fixed cost of a step. With the measured costs per unit (propagation 9.7 ns, doubleton 7.2, row rules 5.1, tightening 5.1, parallel rows 3.4, singleton columns 2.1, dual fixing 1.1; 240, node) and an assumed step cost of 250 microseconds this gives provisional thresholds of 100,000 work units for propagation, 200,000 for tightening and the row rules, 300,000 for parallel rows, 500,000 for the singleton columns and 900,000 for dual fixing.
3. Item: a certified item that was not listed again is skipped; every other item runs today's code. Lines whose sequential dry-run part exceeds a set length (provisional 8,192 entries without an exit) are not certified.
4. Sync: before a bulk step the marked share decides between no sync (marked items go to the host), marked data, or the whole image.
5. Script application (second step): on the device when the script touches more than a set share of the nonzeros, else on the host.

Fixed costs against it (one H200, Stage 0 report): launch with synchronisation 9.0 microseconds, kernel with read-back 13.8, compaction or reduce 23 to 46, sort of 1e3 to 1e5 elements 94 to 501, ordered hand-back at most about 141. A bulk step is 2 to 6 launches, one read-back, one compaction and the sync, which I put at 100 to 250 microseconds; this is an estimate, not a measurement.

What the rule leaves on the host, with the measured size (240, Mac seconds, my script): at a threshold of 100,000 work units the unselected lists and calls are 82% of the steps and 6.8% of the rule seconds (17.7% between 5e4 and 5e5 nonzeros, 1.9% from 1e6). Calls below 20,000 work units are 64.9% of the calls and 0.6% of the engine seconds. unitcal_7 (1,363 of 1,383 calls below 20,000 units) stays on the host by this rule.
identity_rule:
With and without a GPU, between GPU types, between runs, with any thresholds, sync choice and kernel scheduling: everything is equal bit for bit. That covers the reduced model, the record stack, the hash, the state hash after every phase, and every statistic except seconds and the new device and transfer counters. The reason is structural, not a tolerance: the device produces (a) arrays with one definition (state build, keys, sort orders, best candidates under a total order, selections that keep the order, the reduced model, the hash) and (b) certificates of visits without effect; every finding is applied by the same host code in the same order in both runs. So the test "device equals host" stays, and every existing check, the 99 wrong engines and the random campaign test the device path against the host path. I agree with the preference for the same bits and this design gives more than was asked: the hybrid rule cannot change a result either.

Between today's engine and the new one: equal bit for bit when both switches are set to today's behaviour (old hash chain, record rule of today). Two differences otherwise.
1. Hash: a new function. Values change, nothing else.
2. Record rule of bound propagation (recommended, optional): best candidate per column and side from the state at the start of the list, in two phases, in every mode. Records are at least as tight as today's. What follows from them (the bounds make_explicit sets, the rows it lists, the stall accounting through budget.found) can differ.

Four modes exist for tests: host (today's loops), reference (the bulk protocol with plain C++ certificates), device, automatic. All four must give the same phase hashes on every instance.

With device application of scripts (second step) the claim stays the same and is tested by comparing every array of the device image with the host state after each replayed script.
data_layout:
Host: state_t unchanged in content (both stores with start, used, capacity, size per line and index, value, twin per slot; row and column scalars; two activities with hi, lo, inf_count, inf_slot, max_term, updates; lists; counters). The large arrays come from a presolve-owned memory resource so that device-built arrays are moved in, huge pages can be requested and Grace Hopper can use managed memory.

Device image (x86): the same arrays with the same slots, 40 bytes per nonzero (index 4, value 8, twin 8 in each orientation), 20 bytes of header per line and orientation, about 135 bytes per row and 95 per column in all. Tombstones are index -1 as on the host. Deletions, compaction and rebuild are mirrored by the same operations or by copying marked lines. Summation order of an activity: entry k of a row in storage order goes to lane k mod lanes, lanes = activity_lanes(n), merge by the tree of numerics.hpp; the fold kernels are used at the build and wherever the host sums a row from scratch. Incrementally updated activities are the host's and reach the device as data.

Device-only: row ids and column ids sorted by length class (the load balancing; storage is not reordered); two uint16_t arrays of infinite-term counts derived from the host's counts, saturating, a saturated row is not certified; listed and stale flags; certificate (1 byte) and w0 (4 bytes) per listed item; candidate and sort scratch. Peak during the build: 28 bytes per nonzero more.

Not on the device: work lists (the host uploads a taken list as int32), the record stack, family data that outlives a call.

Journal (host, only while a device is attached, not hashed, read by no rule): one mark byte per row and per column with bits for scalars, entries and layout, and two lists of marked indices.

Hand-over, x86: host to device by marked records through pinned staging, with the integer arrays derived on the device; device to host whole arrays after the state build, otherwise flags, keys, orders and records. Grace Hopper: one managed slab, preferred location device, accessed-by host, no mirror, no journal copy; forced on x86 for tests.
verification:
1. Certificate audit (new, in assertion builds and in the campaign): every certified skip is also executed by today's visit code and must change no counter of the state, no list, no record and no activity of the row, and spend exactly w0. This turns every model of the campaign into a test of every certificate, without a GPU.
2. Device against reference: every array a kernel produces (state arrays, certificates, w0, keys, sort order, records, selections, reduced model, hash) is compared with the plain C++ form on the 240, the 40 testbed instances, the 24 hand-made models of the state-build review and campaign models. For throughput many random models are packed into one block-diagonal model for the array comparisons; whole presolves on the device run on a sample.
3. Mode equality: phase hashes equal between host, reference, device forced at every size, and automatic, on the 240 and the testbed; also with the three sync choices, with each threshold forced low and high, and with kernel scheduling variants.
4. Mirror: in assertion builds the whole device image is compared with the host state after every sync and after every mirrored storage operation.
5. Oracle, structure check and crush check: unchanged, since the results are the host's.
6. Wrong engines: the 99 stay. New ones, each caught by a named check: a certificate that ignores the infinite-term count, the integer rounding, the error guard or the stale flag; a wrong w0; a walk without the listed-again test; a state operation without its journal mark; a sync that skips a marked column; the record tie to the larger row; a key that depends on storage order; an unstable sort; a hash sum without the position key.
7. Determinism: the hash sequence compared across repeated runs, a second GPU type, both memory paths (managed forced on x86, then a Grace Hopper node) and with other jobs on the node.
8. Review rules of cuOpt PR 2372: tests with integer and mixed column types, the single-infinity case (x1 + x2 + x3 <= 10 with x3 free), counts in separate uint16_t arrays, no second block reduction for the counts, and every kernel variant timed against the current one before it replaces it.
9. Overheads in every run: seconds of upload, download, sync, kernels and waiting, bytes moved, bulk steps, certified and visited items per family, added to overheads.csv.

milestones.name: M0 Host form of the bulk protocol (no CUDA)
milestones.content: Each family's visit split into a pure evaluation and an application; certificates and the ordered walk in plain C++ (reference mode); certificate audit; journal hooks; the new hash and the two-phase record rule behind switches; the new counters. The convention for the unbuilt column rules is fixed here.
milestones.gate: With both switches at today's behaviour: hashes and all per-family counts equal to today's engine on the 240 and the 40 testbed instances; audit without a violation on those and on the campaign. With the record rule on: remaining nonzeros, rows and columns against today's engine on the 240 and the testbed, geometric mean and every instance below 0.995 explained; summed time within 5% of today's per size class. All wrong engines caught.

milestones.name: M1 Device foundation and state build
milestones.content: Memory resource with the pinned and the managed path; state_t from moved-in arrays; the device state build integrated with the fold kernels; whole download; the hash on the device; measurement of the crossover with a warm context.
milestones.gate: Every state array bit-equal on the 240, the testbed and the hand-made models; mode equality of the phase hashes; state build at least 1.8 times faster end to end from 1.3e6 nonzeros; no instance slower than the host path by more than the larger of 5% and 2 ms; untouched below the threshold.

milestones.name: M2 Mirror and the families without chains
milestones.content: Journal sync and derived arrays; mirrored compaction and rebuild; certificates for tightening and dual fixing; keys, sort and links of the parallel rows; collection for the doubleton rule.
milestones.gate: Device arrays equal to the reference with the device forced at every size; mode and sync equality; time against M1 per size class (below 2e5, 2e5 to 1e6, 1e6 to 1e7, above 1e7), nothing slower by the same rule.

milestones.name: M3 The cascade families
milestones.content: Propagation kernels (row certificate, column records) from the load-balanced structure; row-rule and singleton-column certificates; simple probing's row tests once that family is merged.
milestones.gate: As M2, plus the tests of the PR 2372 review rules and a kernel benchmark against at least one scheduling variant.

milestones.name: M4 Output, thresholds, determinism
milestones.content: Reduced model on the device, optional device-resident result for the cuOpt adapter; all thresholds measured and fixed by the rule of AS-307; second GPU type; managed path forced on x86.
milestones.gate: Acceptance criteria 1 to 7 on the 240 and the testbed with the base plan.

milestones.name: M5 Script application on the device
milestones.content: Replay library (row replay, column replay, first-touch list builder, record gather) for dual fixing, make_explicit, the start step, tightening edits, parallel-row merges, zero-cost singleton columns and the substitution of alias batches; built per script kind where the host application is above 2% of the hybrid time of a size class.
milestones.gate: Device image equal to the host state after every replayed script; mode equality; time against M4 on the instances from 1e6 nonzeros and on the nine large ones.

milestones.name: M6 The nine designed column rules in the split form
milestones.content: Each rule written once as evaluation plus application with its certificate, as host rule in index order as designed, with its validity review and wrong engines; its kernel on the infrastructure of M2 and M3. Can run beside M1 to M5 once M0 exists.
milestones.gate: The gates of the Stage 1c plan for each rule, plus mode equality with the device forced.

milestones.name: M7 Acceptance run
milestones.content: All criteria on the 240, the 40 testbed instances and inside cuOpt; a functional run on Grace Hopper.

acceptance:
1. Every part of the table is classified, and each part left on the host carries a measured share from a run of the finished engine, not from this plan.
2. Device share of the work, counted in work units by the new counters, on the instances from 1e6 nonzeros of the 240 and on the nine large ones: tightening at least 85% certified, propagation at least 90% with the record rule (70% without), row rules at least 60% of the work and 85% of the visits, all parallel-row keys and full sorts, the whole state build, output and hash.
3. Host application left: for each family at most 2% of the hybrid time of each size class, or script application on the device is built for it.
4. Time of the hybrid path against the host path of the same build, minimum of three alternating runs, node of the stored runs: from 1e6 nonzeros (30 of the 240 and the nine large) the summed time is at most 0.5 times; from 2e5 to 1e6 at most 0.75 times; below the model threshold at most 1.02 times. These factors are my projection and may have to be set again by the owner after milestone 1.
5. Nothing slower: no instance of the 240 or the testbed is slower than the host path by more than the larger of 5% and 2 ms.
6. Identity: phase hashes equal between host, reference, device forced and automatic on the 240, the 31 and the nine; equal on a second GPU type, on both memory paths and in ten repeated runs.
7. Reductions: against today's engine the geometric mean of remaining nonzeros, rows and columns is at least 0.999 on the 240 and on the testbed, every instance below 0.995 explained; against the HiGHS ladder reference not below today's 1.002.
8. Campaign: one billion random models through the reference mode with the audit, ten million through the device (packed), all wrong engines caught.
9. Overheads reported in every run; a build without CUDA and the standalone build pass everything.
reductions_lost:
None by construction in the base plan: every reduction is found and applied by today's code in today's order, and the device only removes visits that do nothing.

The one place where the reduced model can differ from today's is the record rule of bound propagation, if the owner takes it. A record is then at least as tight as today's, so the bounds that become explicit are at least as tight, by up to one step (1000 feasibility tolerances by default). I expect equal or slightly more reductions; I did not measure it. It is measured in milestone 0 on the host alone: remaining nonzeros, rows and columns with the switch on against off on the 240 and the 40 testbed instances, and the count of calls that stop on their budget (2 propagation calls on the 240 today).

If the owner refuses it, nothing is lost in reductions; the host then keeps 21.3% of the propagation work instead of 4.8% (240, my probe).

The new hash changes no reduction.
risks: The speed gain on x86 has a ceiling set by host memory and by the applications left on the host. My projection (about 2.5 times on the 240, 2.0 to 2.4 on the nine large, up to about 3 to 4 with huge pages and script application) is arithmetic on measured shares with an assumed 3 to 5% for kernels and sync; no device step of this design was run.

A certificate is only sound if every change of something a visit reads puts the item on the family's list again. I checked this by reading for the row rules and propagation; for the singleton-column family only in part. The audit is the safety net; a family whose certificate cannot be made sound stays on the host.

The mirror on x86 (journal, sync, derived arrays, mirrored compaction and rebuild) is the largest piece of new code without a rule in it, and Grace Hopper does not need it. A missing journal mark gives a wrong certificate; the full image comparison in assertion builds is what catches it.

Dry-run kernels with one thread per line balance badly on long lines, and a sequential part on one GPU thread is slow (the research report quotes cuPSLP section 2.2: 174 ms for a sum of 2.4 million numbers on one A100 thread). The block forms and the length cap are needed early, and the cap sends work back to the host.
Where a host visit is already O(1) (row rules, dual fixing) the device share counts in work units and hardly in seconds; the acceptance criteria must not be read as speed.

Script application for alias batches has to reproduce the column layout that move_entry leaves (appends, doubled capacity, moves to the end of the store). If that proves too costly the alternative is a rebuild after each batch, which changes storage order and with it activity bits.

nvcc must give the host's results for fma, ceil, floor, round and the division with contraction off; this is still unchecked (already marked so in the Stage 1b design). The fold kernels are designed, not built.
The stable radix sort and the order-preserving selection are CUB properties; a library version that changed them would break equality, which the array comparisons would show.
cuOpt's load-balanced kernels are not compiled in this tree; I did not read them and take their structure from the research and inventory reports.
All thresholds and the model threshold are provisional and come from host seconds of a Mac and fixed costs of one H200.
Below the model threshold the GPU does nothing; 'better than HiGHS from 50,000 nonzeros' rests on the host path there.
open_for_owner: Is 'the device tests everything, the host applies the findings in today's order' a complete GPU acceleration in your sense? For the cascades the application is order-dependent by today's definition. For tightening, dual fixing, merges and substitution it is parallel; the plan moves it to the device (M5) only where it is measured above 2% of the hybrid time. You may want all of it, or none.

The record rule of bound propagation (best candidate, two phases). With it the device takes 95.1% of the propagation work, without it 78.6% (240). It is the only change that can alter a reduced model.
The new hash, which replaces every stored hash once; or the old chain on the host at 5.5% of the seconds.

Host memory for the state: huge pages behind the large arrays, state_t taking moved-in arrays, and whether presolve may take the model's CSR arrays instead of copying them. This decides more of the gain on x86 than any kernel.
The model threshold: I propose 2e5 nonzeros provisionally and a measurement in M1. Do you want the device used below it even where it does not pay?
Inside cuOpt: may the adapter hand over the model and take the reduced model as device arrays, so that the upload and the last download disappear?
Order of work: M0 first, then the remaining nine column rules in the split form beside the device milestones (my recommendation), or the device milestones first.

If you want the applications of the cascades on the device too, today's order has to be replaced by rounds from one state, with a new reference engine and more rounds. That is outside this design; say so before M3.
The time factors of the acceptance (0.5 from 1e6 nonzeros, 0.75 from 2e5) are projections; they should be set again after M1.
Grace Hopper: the plan keeps it functional only until the end, as decided on 2026-11-27. The design gains most there (no mirror, no second copy).
unsure: Whether 'not listed again since the take' is a complete test of 'nothing the visit reads has changed' in every family. My probe counts by the pending bit of the family's own row list; it shows how many visits are clean, not that the test is sound.

The certifiable share of tightening and of the singleton-column family: the figures I use (91.4% and 97.9% of the work outside finding visits, 240) are upper bounds; my probe covers only the row rules and propagation.
The cost of a bulk step and of a sync. 100 to 250 microseconds is put together from Stage 0 figures, not measured.

The split of a finding visit's time into test and application. I used work units and the family's cost per unit, which treats both alike; the host residuals (1.6%, 0.8%, 1.3% of the seconds) are upper bounds on that assumption.
The nine instances above 1e7 nonzeros were not probed (not on this machine). For them I used the stored node totals and the shares of the 30 instances from 1e6 nonzeros.
Whether the best-candidate record rule changes reductions measurably, and what my definition of budget.found for records does to the two propagation calls that stop on their budget today.
Whether the position-keyed sum is acceptable as a determinism hash; it keeps the property that one changed word changes the hash, but I did not analyse collisions further.
Seconds in my threshold tables are the measurement agent's Mac seconds; the node is about 2.3 times slower in the sum and has other shares (state build 31.4% against 22.1%).

I did not read the doubleton and alias-forest code, state_storage.cpp, postsolve.cpp, the simple-probing source, the Stage 1c designs, the device state_build.cu, sweeps.cu or cuOpt's load-balanced kernels; what I say about them comes from the inventory and research reports of this round.
Statements about papers (Sofranac et al., cuPSLP, PaPILO, Blelloch et al.) are quoted from the research report, which read them through a fetch tool; I checked none of them.
